terms.grammar: neuter plural: saxum with the participle of liquefaciō
evidence: Verg. A. 3.576–577: liquefactaque saxa sub aurās cum gemitū glomerat
terms.comment: Vergil’s words for what Etna pours out, which Lewis & Short glosses as lava (s.v. liquefaciō). We have found no single ancient word for it. Once it has cooled it is simply saxum: see the examples.

The Neapolitan word, which Egger proposed taking into Latin to spare a long circumlocution; Morgan–Owens cites him. Its vowel quantities are not established and are left unmarked. Egger also has ignium rīvī, streams of fire (M-O s.v. volcano: erupt).

phrases.latin: quotiēns Cyclōpum effervere in agrōs vīdimus undantem ruptīs fornācibus Aetnam, flammārumque globōs liquefactaque volvere saxa!
phrases.english: how often have we seen Etna boil over from her burst furnaces onto the Cyclopes’ fields, and roll out balls of flame and molten rock!

phrases.latin: Hoc saxum nigrum ōlim liquefactum dē monte dēflūxit.
phrases.english: This black rock once ran down the mountain as lava.

phrases.latin: Nōlī appropinquāre: saxa liquefacta etiamnunc fervent.
phrases.english: Don’t go near: the lava is still hot.

sources: Lewis & Short: liquefacio · Lewis & Short: saxum
